standfirst: The United States and Iran traded fire around the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend — the first direct exchange since the strait closed — and Washington is weighing a second round.
The Fed chair used Jackson Hole to say the inflation job is unfinished, and Asian chip stocks spent Monday deciding they did not care.

The week the AI build-out stopped being an equity story and became a price story: Nvidia sold $96.2bn of it, memory swallowed two-thirds of next year's cloud hardware budget, and a new Fed chair stood up at Jackson Hole and blamed the central bank for 65 months of inflation. Elsewhere, Iceland shut the door on Brussels, France's second quarter turned out not to have grown at all, and the Himalayan flood toll passed 750.
The Nepal–Tibet flood toll passed 750 overnight with more than 3,000 still missing, and Sony and Warner sued Anthropic and its two founders personally over how Claude was trained.
Kevin Warsh used a symposium about payments to give an inflation speech, told markets he is done with forward guidance, and left a September rate rise on the table.
A federal judge told the Pentagon it cannot blacklist an AI company for refusing to build what it asked for.
Nvidia beat its own guidance by five billion dollars and guided the October quarter to $108bn, then told investors the memory bill will take three points off its margin.
Dolly Parton died in Nashville at 80, and the flags come down until Tuesday.
Treasury's long-trailed Iran package finally landed — 78 designations, 22 of them Chinese shell companies, and not one Chinese oil buyer among them.
Washington's largest-ever economic offensive against Iran is due at two o'clock this afternoon, and nothing has been published yet.

The United States put a 50% tariff on Canadian goods under a dormant 1930 statute, and Canada walked out of the talks. Chief Justice Roberts, acting alone, let the East Wing ballroom go back up. And Korean chip exports nearly tripled in twenty days — the AI buildout is now visible in a G20 country's national accounts.
Trade talks with Canada collapsed and 50% tariffs took effect Saturday; Ottawa retaliates dollar for dollar on September 8.
Treasury put a name on the Iran policy: Scott Bessent said out loud that the goal is to collapse the regime.
Three Fed officials voted to raise rates in July — the minutes released Wednesday show the hawks are not a fringe.
The UAE cut off all trade and financial dealings with Iran overnight, after saying two ballistic missiles were fired from Iranian territory at shipping.
Nvidia agreed to guarantee the lease and power payments behind OpenAI's eight-gigawatt Ohio campus, putting the chipmaker's balance sheet underneath its own biggest customer.

Stripe agreed to pay more than $7bn — by far its largest deal — for the AI-model gateway OpenRouter, as Jared Kushner met Hamas's top negotiator in Egypt for the first such encounter since last year's Gaza ceasefire.

The American blockade of Iran stopped being a tactic this week and became the policy, with the president musing aloud about annexing the Strait of Hormuz and the Treasury promising economic isolation “like the world has never seen.” Underneath it, a quieter week of records: Europe's hottest June–July ever and four great rivers at their lowest, a $60bn all-stock deal closing, and a Fed still arguing about whether to raise rates into a consumer-confidence collapse.

President Trump vowed to declare the Strait of Hormuz “a territory of the United States,” an extraordinary escalation as tankers came under attack in the strait and markets absorbed a weak 30-year Treasury auction and a Broadcom AI-debt scare.

US stocks closed at a record high on cooling inflation, even as strong earnings from Cisco, Applied Materials and Cerebras were met with falling share prices — investors are grading AI infrastructure spending on a curve of pure perfection.
